title: Appendix B: Four Practical System Designs

sections.title: Deciding When to Assemble the Timeline
The Provider Is the Capacity Limit
Identifying the Records and Their Owners

html:
A URL shortener, a social timeline, and a notification service can each begin with an API, a database, and a background worker. Yet those three systems reach their limits in different places. The shortener has to serve old links quickly while allowing their owners to disable them. The timeline has to show recent posts without making one popular author delay everyone else. A notification service has to deliver a login code before it expires, even when marketing campaigns are filling the provider’s allowance.

The fourth design is an internal change-validation platform. Its main concern is authority: a deployment may have passed policy review this morning, but that policy could change before the pipeline runs tonight. A record of an earlier approval cannot answer whether the deployment is permitted now.

We’ll build each design from its requirements, choose a plausible starting architecture, and examine the failures that would cause us to revise it. The numbers are illustrative and belong to the example workloads. A production design needs the same calculations repeated with its own traffic, storage, provider contracts, and recovery tests.

Using the Five Questions

Chapter 14 returned to five questions: what the application promises, which work a request creates, what survives interruption, how limits are handled, and which evidence changes the design. For each of the four systems, we can use those questions to select the initial components and then decide whether additional machinery is justified. A queue, cache, or another service should earn its place by meeting a stated requirement.

A URL Shortener

Imagine printing a short URL on the tickets for a conference. Months later, someone follows it and expects to reach the page the organizer chose. A second organizer might create another short link to that same page because they want separate usage reports. Either organizer may later disable their link. Those ordinary actions already tell us a great deal about the data model.

The Product Contract

Each successful creation returns a durable code bound to one owner and one destination. The code is never reassigned to another destination, even after the original link is disabled. A repeated creation with the same operation identity and parameters returns the original code. Using the same identity with different parameters is a conflict.

For redirects, our example uses a 200-millisecond p95 objective under normal load. A disabled link must stop redirecting within thirty seconds under the supported caching policy. That is a correctness and abuse-prevention requirement, so it affects cache TTLs and HTTP response headers as much as the database schema.

Estimating Storage and Lookup Demand

Suppose the service creates 50 million links per month and records about one hundred redirects for every link created. Using a thirty-day month and an assumed peak of five times the average gives the following planning figures.

Five years of creation would occupy about 0.085 percent of that code space. The raw storage estimate excludes indexes, replication, logs, and click history. Redirects are roughly one hundred times as frequent as creations, so the read path deserves most of our attention.

At the assumed peak, a 90-percent cache hit rate leaves about 965 database lookups per second. A 50-percent hit rate leaves roughly 4,823. An empty cache can initially expose the store to nearly all 9,645 requests per second. Those are separate capacity tests. Choosing a cache because the average lookup rate seems large does not establish that the database will survive recovery from a cache outage.

Allocating Codes

The simplest implementation generates a cryptographically random code, tries to insert it under a unique database constraint, and retries on collision. At this creation rate, that can be entirely reasonable. It also avoids depending on a separate block allocator.

An alternative assigns sequential identifier blocks to creation workers. A block of 10,000 covers about 8.6 minutes of creations across the whole fleet at the average rate. Four equally loaded workers would each request another block about every 35 minutes. The unused part of a block can be discarded after a crash because the code space is large.

If consecutive public codes reveal unwanted information about creation sequence, a reversible permutation can obscure the counter before base-62 encoding. A Feistel permutation with cycle walking maps a 42-bit domain into the smaller seven-character code space, preserving uniqueness when the allocator never repeats a counter. It does not make a code unguessable. Private or security-sensitive links need unpredictable tokens with enough entropy and a separate authorization model.

The 42-bit domain is about 1.25 times the code space, so a near-uniform permutation needs roughly 1.25 applications on average. This is an illustrative reversible mapping, not vetted cryptographic protection. Changing the secret can cause a new counter to produce a code already issued under the earlier mapping. The service keeps one mapping for this namespace and relies on the database uniqueness constraint as its final safeguard.

Either allocation scheme needs a database constraint that prevents a code from being issued twice. The schema also ties a creation operation identity to one result.

If the insert returns no row, the service retrieves the stored operation, verifies its owner and canonical destination, and returns the same code only when the parameters agree. A code collision produces a uniqueness error, which the creation path handles by generating another code under the same operation identity. Disabling a link does not free its code. If old link records are purged, a durable reservation or tombstone must still prevent that code from being assigned to another destination.

The Redirect Path and Revocation

The hot path is a bounded lookup keyed by the short code. The application caches a tagged result such as ACTIVE, DISABLED, or ABSENT. It distinguishes a confirmed missing row from a failed database query. A timeout is never cached as an absent link.

Here interpret returns a redirect only for an active result. The cache stores ordinary serializable values. It does not use a process-local sentinel object whose identity could change when serialized by Redis. The code assumes a tested, bounded single-flight implementation and an index-backed database lookup.

Twenty seconds of positive caching fits within the thirty-second disable objective under the stated cache behavior. The disable transaction also initiates invalidation of known copies, although correctness does not depend entirely on successful invalidation. A subsecond revocation promise would require a stronger check or invalidation mechanism. The service uses a temporary redirect with an explicit Cache-Control: no-store header because a permanent cached redirect could outlive disablement. The team tests browsers, proxies, and CDNs against the stated bound.

A destination is untrusted input. The creation API validates permitted URL schemes and applies abuse controls. Link ownership is checked before editing or disabling a code. Possessing a short code alone does not grant authority over its destination.

Failure and Recovery

At 9,645 cache misses per second and five milliseconds of average store occupancy, about 48 lookups are outstanding on average. That estimate excludes queueing and tail latency. The database needs a concurrency limit so a cache outage cannot open unlimited connections. Controlled warming and bounded refill protect the store, with temporary-unavailable results when capacity is exhausted.

Click analytics leave the redirect path through an optional nonblocking handoff. If the queue is full, events may be sampled or dropped under the reporting contract. Approximate click totals must not be described as exact. Security and abuse detection need their own appropriate evidence rather than relying solely on sampled marketing analytics.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & A 90-percent cache hit rate keeps ordinary store traffic below about 1,
000 lookups/s at the assumed 9,645/s peak. Revocation must take effect within thirty seconds.

Condition that tests it & A cache flush, campaign surge, random-code scan, or popular link disable.
Constraint or invariant & Codes are never reassigned. One creation identity has one result. Unknown store outcomes are not interpreted as missing links.
Evidence and uncertainty & The peak factor, hit rate, and record size are estimates. Cold-cache store performance and browser cache behavior remain to be tested.
Signal and evaluation window & Measure cache hits, store concurrency, redirect p95, and disable delay during peak and recovery drills.
Control and decision & Bound store admission and use temporary redirects with controlled TTLs. Revise caching if revocation or cold-cache objectives fail.
Owner and review trigger & The link-service owner owns creation and disablement. Review before increasing traffic or changing cache policy.

A Social Timeline

A person opens a social application to see recent posts from people they follow. The interface feels like one read, but the system must collect posts from many authors and decide whether the viewer is still permitted to see each one. The cost of assembling the timeline can fall when a post is created or when someone opens the page. Those choices have different worst cases.

The Customer Contract and Workload

The first version promises a recent, chronological selection from followed accounts within the page latency objective. Every returned post must pass current visibility rules. The product also declares a bounded freshness interval for ordinary posts and a permitted reduced result while its materialized index is rebuilding. An exact, complete global ordering across millions of followed items is outside this initial contract.

Suppose twenty million daily users each publish two posts and open their timelines ten times a day. Assume the author-weighted average number of followers is 200. This qualification matters because highly active authors may have more followers than typical accounts.

The 128-GB estimate counts only eight-byte identifiers. Redis sorted-set metadata, keys, allocator overhead, indexes, and replication can make the actual memory requirement much greater. The feed team uses that number as a lower bound rather than a memory-sizing result.

At a fleet-wide rate of 92,600 inserts per second, ten million inserts consume about 108 seconds of the entire nominal write capacity. During those 108 seconds, ordinary posts continue arriving. If one large fan-out job occupies a first-in-first-out queue, ordinary posts become stale even while the workers are busy.

Deciding When to Assemble the Timeline

With fan-out on write, the service appends a new post identifier to each follower’s materialized timeline. Reads are cheap, but a popular author creates a large amount of write work. With fan-out on read, each post is stored once, and a reader retrieves posts from followed authors before merging them. That avoids write amplification but can require hundreds of queries for one timeline open.

The example uses a hybrid. Ordinary authors fan out into follower timelines in bounded batches. Authors above a measured follower threshold keep their posts in an author-indexed list, which the feed service merges during reads. A reader following many large accounts still needs a read budget. The product specifies which subset is retrieved when that budget is exhausted and reports reduced coverage rather than claiming the result is complete.

The initial threshold might be a few hundred thousand followers, but it cannot come from the global average. The team measures follower concentration, posting frequency, fan-out cost, and the number of large accounts followed by actual readers. Lowering the threshold protects the write fleet at the expense of read work. Raising it moves that work back into fan-out.

Writing and Reading the Feed

The materialized timeline is an index of post IDs ordered by creation time. The authoritative post body and access rules live in Post Service. A repeated fan-out event adds the same member with the same score, so the stored operation can be idempotent. Workers process followers in bounded chunks and schedule those chunks fairly across authors.

The illustrative redis_atomic_update represents a server-side script or transaction making insertion and trimming one operation for the key. Replaying a post ID with the same source timestamp produces the same final timeline state. If the same ID could be replayed with a different score, that assumption would fail and the worker would need a version check.

The read path retrieves a bounded number of materialized IDs, pulls recent posts from the selected high-follower authors, and merges them using a stable timestamp-and-ID ordering. Post Service then returns only posts currently visible to that viewer. The application overfetches to compensate for deleted and unauthorized candidates, with an explicit cap on work.

A cap on high-follower pulls can omit some eligible recent posts. The service measures that loss of coverage and offers pagination or a more expensive retrieval path when the product requires greater completeness. It cannot promise the newest posts from every followed account while silently ignoring some authors after reaching its pull budget.

Visibility, Deletion, and Rebuilding

A follower can block an author, leave a private group, or unfollow an account after a post has already entered the materialized feed. Its identifier is then a stale candidate. The read path checks current permission before returning the post. Deletion creates a tombstone in the authoritative store, and background cleanup later removes stale IDs. Permission revocation does not wait for that cleanup.

Following also needs a declared rule. A new follow could include the account’s recent posts or only those published afterward. Unfollowing must affect the next read, even if old identifiers still appear in Redis. A pagination cursor must tolerate follow changes without treating an omitted post as proof that it was never published.

If the Redis fleet fails, the post store and follow graph are the source for rebuilding timelines. The service limits rebuild concurrency and may serve a reduced feed while catching up. Rebuilding every user’s complete feed at once could transfer a Redis failure into a database or network incident. Recovery tests keep new posts arriving so the team measures its actual additional catch-up throughput.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & A hybrid feed permits recent chronological reads while preventing high-follower authors from monopolizing fan-out workers.
Condition that tests it & A popular account posts at peak, or a reader follows hundreds of high-follower accounts.
Constraint or invariant & Fan-out and read work are bounded. Every returned post passes a current visibility check. Replayed IDs do not duplicate materialized entries.
Evidence and uncertainty & The author-weighted mean of 200 followers is assumed. The follower skew, memory overhead, and acceptable read coverage need measurement.
Signal and evaluation window & Track post-to-visible p95 and p99, oldest fan-out age, pulls per read, rebuild rate, and retrieval coverage during peak and recovery tests.
Control and decision & Tune the fan-out threshold and scheduling budget from workload tests. Reduce read breadth explicitly when the pull budget is exhausted.
Owner and review trigger & The feed team owns latency and freshness. Post Service owns visibility. Review on workload growth or failed permission drills.

A Notification Service

A one-time login code arriving six minutes after it was requested may be useless. A marketing email arriving six minutes late may be perfectly acceptable. Both can use the same provider, but they need different deadlines, admission rules, and recovery policies.

What Is Actually Guaranteed?

An accepted notification request becomes a durable task. Repeated submissions with the same operation identity and parameters create one logical task. The sender records the provider’s response, including uncertain outcomes, and distinguishes provider acceptance from recipient delivery. A provider can accept a message and later report a bounce. Even a delivery report does not prove that a recipient opened or read it.

An expired login code must not be sent. Marketing messages must satisfy current consent and preference rules at dispatch time, since a customer may unsubscribe after a campaign has been queued. Quiet hours are applied according to message class. Security notifications may have a different policy from promotional mail, and the task records which policy applies.

The Provider Is the Capacity Limit

Suppose an ordinary day has ten million notifications, or about 116 per second on average. A campaign adds two million promotional messages over ten minutes, or about 3,333 per second. The provider permits 1,000 accepted submissions per second for this account. The campaign alone offers more than three times the total allowance.

The 39.2-minute estimate starts when the campaign begins and assumes promotional workers use their full 850-per-second allocation, even while new messages arrive. After ten minutes, about 1.49 million campaign messages would still be waiting. At 850 per second, finishing them would take another 29.2 minutes. Provider slowdowns, retries, and failed tasks would change the actual duration.

The team reserves 150 submissions per second for transactional traffic with a separate bounded burst allowance. Promotional traffic receives at most 850 per second. Unused transactional capacity could eventually be lent to campaigns if the allocator can reclaim it promptly, but the initial design keeps the classes separate so login latency is easier to predict during a campaign.

The reserve is a sustained rate allocation, enforced by a shared service across every sender. It is more reliable than a simple token bucket whose bulk callers can spend refill tokens between priority arrivals. A total 1,000-per-second rate limit also protects the provider account, and per-producer quotas reject excess work at acceptance. Adding sender workers helps only until these shared limits become binding.

Durable Tasks and Sender States

The API commits one notification task under a stable operation identity. Worker queues separate transactional messages from campaigns. A task records the recipient, template, class, expiry, preference policy, and current state. Workers use expiring leases and versioned claims so an old sender cannot overwrite a newer worker’s result.

A provider submission follows a specific order: check expiry and current preferences, reserve provider capacity, record dispatch intent, send with the original provider idempotency identity, and record the observed outcome. The reservations are coordinated across processes and released only when the provider contract permits the remote attempt to be considered complete.

The methods represent durable conditional transitions, rather than independent in-memory assignments. If a worker crashes after recording intent, the request might never have been sent. If the provider accepted the request but lost the response, the remote effect may already have occurred. Both cases need reconciliation under the same task identity and provider account.

When the provider supports a suitable idempotency key or definitive status lookup, the worker uses that contract to recover. Otherwise, the business must choose how to handle an uncertain outcome. A repeat may cause another message, while refusing to retry may omit a required one. An expired passcode is never automatically turned into a fresh valid code merely because its earlier submission was uncertain.

Definitive temporary failures use bounded backoff with jitter. Retries also consume the shared provider allowance and the retry budget. Permanent template or address errors enter a review or quarantine path with an assigned owner and deadline. The sender monitors the oldest unfinished task by class, not just total queue length or worker use.

Preferences and Fallback Channels

A customer may unsubscribe at 09:00 while marketing mail accepted at 08:00 is still queued. The sender checks current preferences at 09:05 before dispatching. A cached preference value whose freshness exceeds the opt-out contract is unsafe for this decision. The team defines where preference authority lives and how quickly revocation must take effect. A suppressed message is recorded as such, rather than as a delivery failure.

A second provider or channel may help when the first is unavailable. It brings another capacity limit, identity, cost, and consent policy. Sending a login code through SMS after an email timeout can cause both messages to arrive if the email later completes. The product must define whether one code remains valid across channels, how duplicates are handled, and what the customer sees. A fallback provider is useful only after those cases have been tested.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & A 1,
000/s provider allowance can support transactional traffic while a two-million-message campaign is deferred under a separate allocation.

Condition that tests it & Campaign bursts, provider slowdown, sender crash after dispatch, and late preference changes.
Constraint or invariant & Accepted tasks are durable. Expiry and consent are checked at dispatch. Provider acceptance and actual delivery are separate outcomes.
Evidence and uncertainty & A 150/s transactional allocation and 850/s bulk cap are planning values. Provider enforcement windows and idempotency require testing.
Signal and evaluation window & Track oldest task age by class, provider acceptances, unknown attempts, and quota rejections through the campaign and recovery period.
Control and decision & Enforce one shared allowance, reserve transactional capacity, and reconcile uncertain submissions before repeating them.
Owner and review trigger & Notification platform owns dispatch and provider limits. Producing teams own message quotas and consent obligations. Review after failure drills.

A Centralized Change-Validation Platform

An engineer prepares a deployment, and Jenkins reports that the change passed its policy check. Slack warns that the same kind of change is restricted. Jira contains an approval, but nobody can tell whether it applies to the current artifact. Each tool has a different description of the rules, and the deployment pipeline is about to act on one of them.

The first problem here is authority. A policy evaluation records what the rules concluded at a particular time. The system that actually starts a deployment must establish that the intended action is still permitted when execution begins.

Defining the Product Contract

An administrator can publish an immutable policy revision. Exactly one revision is active for each protected environment at a given point in the authoritative store. Each evaluation identifies the submitted artifact, target, actor, input digest, policy revision, evidence, and decision. The enforcement service uses those facts to grant or refuse one specific deployment operation under the current execution policy.

The decision vocabulary has three outcomes. ALLOW means the required evidence supports execution under the evaluated rules. DENY means an applicable rule forbids it. INDETERMINATE means the system cannot establish the answer because required evidence is missing or a dependency is unavailable. The deployment controller refuses protected execution for both DENY and INDETERMINATE, although it can present different explanations and retry procedures.

Slack communicates decisions. Jira supplies approval evidence under its integration contract. Neither can change authoritative policy through a side channel. A change ID, approval link, or idempotency key cannot grant execution permission merely because a caller possesses it.

Identifying the Records and Their Owners

The initial data model distinguishes published policy revisions, the active revision pointer, change inputs, evaluations, and deployment authorizations. Connector observations record which revision an integration has applied. These records change at different times and answer different questions.

A relational database is a reasonable initial authority store because its constraints and transactions can enforce these relationships. Revision numbers are scoped to the environment. Published revisions require append-only write privileges or an equivalent database-enforced rule, and an evaluation cannot change its input identity when a request is retried.

The complete model also stores change ownership and approvals, action-specific authorizations, audit observations, and the durable outbox. A unique request key permits replay of an identical evaluation. If the input digest changes under the same scoped key, the API returns a conflict. Neither this schema nor a stored ALLOW decision establishes current permission to begin a deployment.

Choosing an Initial Architecture

At the stated scale, a modular HTTPS application backed by PostgreSQL is enough for policy publication, evaluation, and authorization. Separate modules own those operations, while a database transaction controls publication of the active revision. A durable outbox and background worker deliver notifications and reconcile connector observations.

Large immutable policy bundles or audit evidence can use object storage such as S3, referenced by revision and verified by digest. Immutable rule bodies may be cached in process memory or Redis, but the protected execution boundary checks authoritative active-revision and revocation evidence. Redis does not become an independent policy publisher.

SQS is suitable for bounded integration tasks and retries. Kafka becomes useful when independent consumers require a retained ordered history and replay. Neither choice changes who may publish policy or authorize a deployment.

The initial request volume is small. Two hundred teams producing ten evaluations per day create 2,000 evaluations daily, or about 0.023 per second averaged over the day. A release window with 1,000 evaluations in five minutes produces 3.33 per second. Reproducible business decisions and transactional correctness matter more than raw database throughput at that volume. Burst rate and external approval latency still require testing, particularly if every step of a deployment begins making a new policy request.

The Revision-17 Failure

Suppose Jenkins evaluated artifact A under revision 17 and received ALLOW. An administrator then publishes revision 18, which prohibits that deployment. Jenkins still has the earlier decision. If it treats the decision as permanent permission, the new restriction cannot prevent the deployment.

The platform separates evaluation from execution authorization. The evaluation remains retrievable as a historical result. Immediately before the protected action, the deployment controller asks whether the exact artifact and configuration, actor, environment, approval evidence, and current policy permit execution. The authorization has a short validity period and applies only to its bound operation.

This is the time-of-check/time-of-use problem from Chapter 10. Even a signed token cannot prove that permission remains valid after revocation if the controller accepts that token offline until expiry. The organization must decide whether newly published restrictions apply to deployments already in progress. A requirement for immediate revocation needs an enforcement protocol that can stop the executor from dispatching further protected steps. A policy that lets an already admitted operation finish has a different contract and should state it.

POST /evaluations
{
  "change_id": "0bbdbf98-9027-4a92-88c4-7d18e9f41067",
  "request_key": "build-184-attempt-1",
  "artifact_sha256": "full-artifact-digest",
  "environment": "production",
  "target_service": "billing-api"
}

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{
  "policy_revision": 17,
  "decision": "ALLOW",
  "input_sha256": "full-canonical-input-digest"
}

The digest strings are placeholders. The production API uses complete validated digests and a documented canonicalization rule. Repeating a request key with identical inputs retrieves the same evaluation. Changing the artifact under that key is an error. Retrieving the response later does not grant execution authority.

Testing Authority and Recovery

The release system refuses new protected execution when the authority store cannot establish the current decision. It returns INDETERMINATE or an equivalent explicit failure, without using an earlier Slack message or cached ALLOW as a fallback. This trades some deployment availability for enforceable policy.

Integrations need independent recovery. Jira can time out during approval lookup, Slack may miss a publication event, and a worker can crash after updating an external connector. Durable operation identities and attempt records support reconciliation. The enforcement service still makes the current execution decision even when connector projections are behind.

The operational dashboard reports the share of protected deployments that passed the current authorization boundary, evaluation latency by outcome, indeterminate results by missing dependency, the active policy revision, connector drift, and the age of unresolved enforcement attempts. An audit compares desired and observed connector revisions without treating drift alone as proof that an unauthorized deployment occurred. That claim requires evidence from the protected execution records.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & A modular policy authority with PostgreSQL can publish revisions and make reproducible deployment decisions at the stated release rate.
Condition that tests it & A policy changes after evaluation, external approval is unavailable, or the enforcement service fails during deployment.
Constraint or invariant & Protected execution requires current authorization for one artifact, actor, target, and policy. An old evaluation cannot grant permission.
Evidence and uncertainty & The 2,
000-evaluation daily workload is illustrative. Approval evidence freshness, revocation timing, and controller cooperation need validation.

Signal and evaluation window & Measure refusal correctness, active-revision consistency, connector drift, indeterminate rate, and authorization latency at release peaks.
Control and decision & Enforce at the protected execution boundary and fail closed on missing authority. Reconcile integrations without granting them policy control.
Owner and review trigger & The policy team owns publication. Security owns authorization rules. Release Engineering owns enforcement. Review after policy changes or drills.

What These Designs Teach Us

The four systems use different diagrams because they make different promises. The shortener needs durable nonreusable codes and measured revocation delay. The timeline needs bounded fan-out and current visibility checks. The notification service needs separate delivery classes and a provider submission contract. The change-validation platform needs policy authority that can refuse execution after an earlier evaluation has become obsolete.

We can identify the required components by following each operation. A redirect creates a cache lookup and perhaps a database read. A social post can create millions of timeline updates. A campaign creates a backlog whose drain rate is limited by an external provider. A policy revision changes which deployment actions are permissible. Once those effects are clear, we can estimate which resource or authority boundary is likely to limit the design.

Recovery also depends on the business effect. A timeline index can be rebuilt from authoritative posts. A disabled short code cannot be reused for another destination. A timed-out provider submission cannot be assumed to have failed. Yesterday’s policy evaluation cannot establish permission to deploy today.

These are applications of the same five-question review from Chapter 14. For an unfamiliar system, we can begin with the user-visible operation, identify its owner and guarantees, estimate the work it creates, and choose components that enforce those requirements. Later measurements or an incident may justify a different design. The recorded assumptions and evidence tell the team when that revision is warranted.
